questions.q: A payment SDK takes your callback and, because of a bug, calls it twice. What is the name for the underlying problem with callbacks that this shows?
questions.explain: Passing a callback hands control of your code to the library. It can call you twice, never, or at odd times. Callback hell is the nesting problem, which is real but shallower. A promise gives control back: you get an object and decide what to do with its single result.
options: Inversion of control: someone else's code decides when and how often your code runs

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A promise settles at most once. The first resolve("ch_1") fulfils it; the later resolve and reject calls are ignored.
options:
paid ch_1
paid ch_2
failed declined

questions.q: The promise is already fulfilled when then is called. What does this print?
questions.explain: Handlers always run later, after the current synchronous code, even when the promise is already settled. That guarantee is what stops the "sometimes synchronous, sometimes not" bug that callbacks allow.

questions.q: A promise was fulfilled a minute ago. Now some code calls .then(handler) on it. What happens?
questions.explain: A settled promise keeps its result. Handlers attached late still receive it, which is different from an event that fires once and is gone.
options: Nothing: the handler missed the event
The handler runs soon after, with the same value
The promise runs its executor again
It throws, because the promise is already settled

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The executor runs synchronously during new Promise, and calling resolve does not stop it, so 3 prints too. Only the then handler waits until the synchronous code (5) is done.

questions.q: Promise order was created with new Promise((resolve) => resolve(payment)), where payment is still pending. Which statement is true?
questions.explain: Resolving with a promise (or thenable) makes your promise follow it: this is adoption. Its fate is decided, so it is resolved, but it stays pending until payment settles, and it can still end up rejected.
options: order is fulfilled with the payment promise object as its value
order is resolved but still pending; it will end up however payment ends up
order is rejected, because you cannot resolve with a promise

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: resolve(payment) locks order to payment, so the following reject is ignored. payment is rejected, and order copies that. "Resolved" does not mean "succeeded".

questions.q: What happens when the executor function passed to new Promise throws an error before calling resolve?
questions.explain: A throw during the executor becomes a rejection. That is why a promisify wrapper calls the SDK inside the executor: a synchronous throw from the SDK then arrives as a rejection like every other failure. A throw in a callback that runs later, such as a timer, is not covered.
options: The error escapes from new Promise and must be caught with try/catch around it
The promise is rejected with that error
The error is silently ignored and the promise fulfils with undefined

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: then never changes the promise it is called on. It returns a new promise, b, fulfilled with the handler's return value. a still holds 1. Handlers run in the order their promises were ready: b's value was already waiting, but it only became fulfilled after a's handler ran, which happened before the last a.then was attached.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The handler has braces and no return, so it returns undefined, and the promise from then is fulfilled with undefined. Either drop the braces or write return.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Returning a promise from a handler makes the promise from then follow it. The next handler receives the final value, 20 ms later, never the promise itself. This is what lets chains stay flat.

questions.q: Inside a then handler, code calls saveOrder(order), which returns a promise, but does not return it. What goes wrong?
questions.explain: The chain only knows about what the handler returns. A promise started and not returned is a floating promise: nobody waits for it and nobody handles its errors. Return it, or await it.
options: Nothing; the chain waits for every promise created inside a handler
The chain moves on at once without waiting, and if saving fails, the rejection is not handled by the chain
The chain is rejected with a TypeError

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A rejection skips every step without a rejection handler (A, B). The catch handles it and returns undefined, which fulfils the chain again, so D runs.
questions.code:
Promise.reject(new Error("out of stock"))
  .then(() => console.log("A"))
  .then(() => console.log("B"))
  .catch((error) => console.log("C", error.message))
  .then(() => console.log("D"));
options:
A
B
C out of stock
D

questions.q: Why is .catch((error) => console.log(error)) in the middle of a checkout chain usually a bug?
questions.explain: A rejection handler's outcome follows the same rules as then: returning (even implicitly) fulfils the chain. If it cannot fix the problem, it must rethrow after logging.
options: It returns undefined, which turns the failure into a success, so the following steps run with undefined
catch can only be the last step of a chain

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Throwing inside a catch keeps the chain rejected, now with the new error. The { cause } option keeps the original error attached, so the last handler can see both.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The second argument of then only handles a rejection of the promise before it. An error thrown by the first argument, in the same step, rejects the next promise, which the catch on the next line handles.
options:
handler 1: empty order
handler 2: empty order

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: finally ignores its handler's return value and passes the original result through. Only a throw (or a rejected promise) in the handler changes the outcome.
questions.code:
const result = await Promise.resolve("order 7 paid").finally(() => "cleaned up");
console.log(result);

questions.q: A payment promise is fulfilled. Its .finally handler throws new Error("could not release lock"). What does the promise returned by finally do?
questions.explain: finally passes the result through unless its own handler fails. Then the cleanup error replaces the result, just like an exception thrown in a finally block of try/catch.
options: It is fulfilled with the payment value; errors in finally are ignored
It is rejected with "could not release lock"
It is fulfilled with the error object

questions.q: What argument does a .finally handler receive?
questions.explain: finally is for cleanup that must happen either way, so it gets no argument. If you need the value or the error, use then or catch.
options: None: it does not know whether the promise succeeded

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: An async function always returns a new promise. Returning a plain value fulfils it with that value.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: return charge() hands the promise out of the function before it rejects, so the try block is already finished and its catch never runs. return await waits inside the try, so the rejection is thrown there and caught.
options:
payA rejected: card declined
handled in payB

handled in payA
handled in payB

payA rejected: card declined
payB rejected: card declined

handled in payA
payB rejected: card declined

questions.q: What makes a value a thenable?
questions.explain: Only a callable then counts. await, Promise.resolve and resolve() call it with a resolve and a reject function. { then: "tomorrow" } is just an object.
options: It has a then property of any type
It has a then property that is a function
It is an instance of a class that extends Promise

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Nothing runs when the object is created. await sees a then method, calls it, and continues with the value passed to resolve. Query builders use exactly this to run a query only when it is awaited.

questions.q: An async function returns { task: "Call supplier", then(next) { this.next = next; } }. The caller awaits it. What happens?
questions.explain: Any object with a callable then is adopted. Its then stores the resolve function instead of calling it, so the promise stays pending forever, with no error. Do not name a method then unless you mean it.
options: A TypeError: objects cannot have a then method
The await never finishes: the object's then is called as a thenable and never calls resolve

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A then property that is not a function does not make a thenable, so the object itself becomes the value.
options: TypeError: then is not a function

questions.q: In a promisify wrapper, why is the SDK function called inside the new Promise executor rather than before it?
questions.explain: The executor catches a synchronous throw and rejects the promise. Callers of the wrapper then only need await + try/catch (or .catch), never a second try around the call itself.
options: If the SDK throws synchronously, the executor turns the throw into a rejection, so callers see every failure the same way
The SDK can only see resolve from inside
Calling it outside would run it twice

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The wrapper forwards its own this with fn.call(this, …). Called as sms.sendAsync(…), this is sms. Called as a plain function, this is undefined (module code is strict), so reading this.sender throws a TypeError inside the timer callback... except that it happens inside the SDK's arrow function, which reads this from send: undefined.sender. The throw is in a timer callback, not the executor? No: this.sender is read when the timer fires, so it would crash. Read the explanation below the question.

questions.q: What is wrong with return new Promise((resolve) => { chargeCard().then(resolve); });?
questions.explain: Wrapping an existing promise in new Promise adds nothing and loses errors, because nobody calls reject. Just return chargeCard(), or return chargeCard().then(transform).
options: Nothing, it is the recommended way to return a promise
It is the explicit construction anti-pattern: if chargeCard rejects, the outer promise never settles and the rejection is unhandled
resolve cannot be passed as a callback

questions.q: When does a rejected promise count as unhandled?
questions.explain: JavaScript gives you until the end of the current task and its microtasks to attach a handler. A handler attached later, such as in a setTimeout, comes too late: the rejection has already been reported, and Node.js crashes by default.
options: As soon as it is created with no handler, before any other line runs
When it is still without a rejection handler after the current piece of work (the task and its microtasks) is finished
Only when the process is about to exit
Never, if it was created inside an async function

questions.q: This runs in Node.js. What does it print?
questions.explain: The catch is attached in the same synchronous block that created the rejected promise, so it is handled in time and the unhandledRejection event never fires.
options:
unhandled: refund failed
handled: refund failed

questions.q: What does Node.js do by default when a promise rejection is unhandled?
questions.explain: Since Node.js 15 the default mode is throw: an unhandled rejection crashes the process like an uncaught exception, because an error nobody saw may have left work half done.
options: It prints a warning and keeps running
It prints the error and exits with a non-zero exit code

questions.q: In the checkout, the stock is reserved and then the card is declined. What should the checkout do before reporting the failure?
questions.explain: Step 1 changed something, so when step 2 fails, step 1 must be undone or the items look sold forever. Rejecting with { cause } tells the caller what failed and why.
options: Nothing; the payment failure is reported and that is enough
Release the reserved stock (compensation), then reject with an error that has the payment error as its cause
Retry the card until it succeeds

questions.q: The card was charged, then sending the SMS receipt fails. Which design fits the checkout's rules?
questions.explain: A notification is not worth failing a paid order for. Recovering is right here, but it must be visible: write the failure into the result or a log so someone can act on it. An empty catch hides it.
options: Reject the whole checkout; the customer will retry and pay again
Complete the order and record that the receipt was not sent, so it can be resent
Ignore the error completely with an empty catch

questions.q: A test calls checkout(services, order) without await and then checks services.stock. Why can it pass even when the checkout is broken?
questions.explain: Without await, the test only starts the work. Its assertions run immediately, and any later rejection happens after the test has finished. Asynchronous tests must await the result.
options: The check runs before any of the asynchronous steps have happened, so it looks at the untouched starting state
checkout runs synchronously when called from a test
The promise rejects silently in tests

questions.q: Tests use this trick to inspect a rejection. What does it print?
questions.explain: The rejection handler returns the error, which fulfils the new promise with it. A success is mapped to null, so a test can tell "rejected as expected" from "wrongly succeeded".

questions.q: Finish promisify(fn): it returns a function that calls fn with the same arguments plus an error-first callback, keeps this, and returns a promise that rejects on error and fulfils with the result.
questions.explain: Return a normal function (not an arrow) so it has its own this, and forward it with fn.call(this, …). The callback decides between reject and resolve.
questions.expected:
SpeedNG booked parcel 7
failed: too heavy: 45 kg

questions.q: Rewrite the nested chain as one flat chain with a single .catch at the end. It must print the same thing.
questions.explain: Each handler returns the next promise, so the chain waits for it and passes its value on. One catch at the end covers every step, which the nested version could not do.

questions.q: The catch in loadRates logs and silently turns the failure into undefined. Change it so it logs, then rejects with a new error "could not load rates" whose cause is the original error. The caller's output should become the expected one.
questions.explain: A rejection handler that returns fulfils the chain. To keep failing, it must throw. Wrapping with { cause } adds context without losing the original error.
questions.expected:
log: rates service timeout
could not load rates (cause: rates service timeout)

questions.q: Finish book(room): hold the room, then take the deposit. If the deposit fails, release the hold and rethrow the error. Use async/await.
questions.explain: The try must wrap an awaited call (return await), or the rejection happens after the try has finished. The catch undoes the hold (compensation) and rethrows so the caller still learns about the failure.

questions.q: A warehouse SDK calls back with several results: callback(error, sku, qty). Finish promisifyMany so the promise fulfils with an array of all the results.
questions.explain: A promise holds one value, so several callback results must be packed into one: a rest parameter ...results collects them into an array.

questions.q: Make query() a thenable: add a then(resolve) method that resolves with the products matching every filter, so await runs the query.
questions.explain: await calls any then method it finds, passing a resolve function. Nothing runs until then, so filters can be added first.

questions.q: The refund promise is created now but only awaited after other work. Attach a handler right away so the rejection is never unhandled, and still print the failure after the other work. Keep the await wait(20).
questions.explain: The starter rejects after 5 ms while nothing is listening, so it is an unhandled rejection that crashes Node.js and fails the terminal run. Attaching both handlers immediately turns the outcome into a value you can await whenever you like.
questions.expected:
other work done
refund: refund failed

questions.q: getPrice calls back synchronously on a cache hit and later on a miss. Rewrite it to return a promise, so both calls print after.
questions.explain: Promise handlers always run after the current synchronous code, even when the value is ready at once. So the order is the same for a cache hit and a cache miss.

questions.q: Which of these does not check its argument for a then method and adopt it?
questions.explain: Adoption happens wherever a promise is resolved with a value: await, Promise.resolve, the executor's resolve, returning from a handler or an async function. Logging a value just prints it.

questions.q: In Node.js, which is the best way to read a file with await?
questions.explain: Node ships promise versions of its APIs (node:fs/promises, node:timers/promises). Use util.promisify or your own wrapper only for callback APIs that have no promise version. Wrapping the sync version still blocks the thread.
